newsitem.title: USA: Test may predict fate in colorectal cancer.
newsitem.headline: Test may predict fate in colorectal cancer.

text.p: A team of doctors reported in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine that they may have identified a physical marker that predicts if a person with colon cancer is likely to respond to treatment.
The marker, known as "deleted in colorectal cancer" or DCC, is a chunk of the 18th chromosome found in virtually all cells in the body.

Using 132 tumour samples taken from volunteers, a group led by Dr. David Shibata of New England Deaconess Hospital found that conventional treatments tended to work best when a patient had the normal two copies of DCC in each cell.
For example, among people with moderately advanced colorectal cancer, the five-year survival rate was 94 percent for people with two copies of DCC, but 62 percent for those with one DCC copy missing.
When the tumour was more advanced, the survival rate was 59 percent with both copies of DCC compared to 33 percent when one copy was missing.

The results showed that DCC appeared to be a piece of genetic material whose normal job was to protect the body from tumours. "It seems highly relevant that the absence of DCC in tumours is linked to poor survival among patients with colorectal cancer," the Shibata team said.
The findings may lead to a test that helps doctors predict who is most likely to benefit from standard cancer treatments, they said.
Colorectal cancer strikes about 138,000 Americans each year and about 55,000 people die from it annually, according to the American Cancer Society.
